claims.statement: Only OAuth mode constructs the account pool; its provider selects an account during request preparation, strips client Authorization and x-api-key, injects the selected token as Authorization: Bearer, and returns the account ID for inference error attribution.

The credential JSON maps account IDs to type, access and refresh tokens, and an absolute Unix expiration in milliseconds; enrollment and refresh compute it from a clock reading plus the OAuth expires_in seconds multiplied by 1000.

The shipped single-replica Recreate deployment mounts the ReadWriteOnce credential PVC at /data and is configured to use /data/credentials.json, so a replacement pod using the same PVC and path reloads the persisted credentials. CREDENTIAL_FILE can override the effective path.

Startup uses the explicit providers list when nonempty and all stored IDs otherwise; it recreates every member as Available and resets the round-robin cursor, so cooldown and disablement do not survive pod replacement.

Explicit providers specify startup membership, not a live allowlist: admin enrollment can add an unlisted member that will not rejoin at restart, and deleting an ID still listed in configuration does not stop startup from listing it even without credentials.
Pending enrollment PKCE state is process-local, keyed by OAuth state, subject to a ten-minute age check and consumed before code exchange; a replacement pod cannot complete an old pending enrollment.

A missing credential file is created as empty JSON; with the shipped empty providers list, the resulting pool has no selectable accounts and is unhealthy. Failure to read or parse an existing file fails startup rather than clearing it.

Each nonempty selection advances the atomic round-robin start once, scans at most one lap, skips disabled, missing-status and still-cooling members, lazily promotes elapsed cooldowns, and disables and skips an eligible member whose credential is missing.
If selection cannot supply a token it returns PoolExhausted with status counts; the provider passes the error up and the proxy responds HTTP 503.

Health summarizes recorded status, reporting healthy for a nonempty all-available pool, degraded for a partly available pool, and unhealthy for no available members. An elapsed cooldown can still appear as cooling_down with zero seconds until selection visits it; exhaustion counts treat elapsed cooldowns as available without promoting them. Health does not validate credentials.
The public /health handler returns HTTP 200 even for unhealthy pool status in the body; /admin/pool returns the same pool summary.

Only an inference 429 containing a known case-insensitive quota phrase is classified as QuotaExceeded; it sets a local cooldown using cooldown_secs (7200 as shipped), not an upstream reset time, and can trigger a new account selection and resend. A generic inference 429 is returned without a cooldown or retry.
Inference 401/403 is permanent: the proxy reports it to disable the account and immediately returns the upstream error without failing over for that request.

The quota-failover inference-attempt budget is startup membership size with a minimum of one and is not resized by live membership changes. A quota response on the last allowed attempt is returned, but failure to select on a further allowed attempt gives HTTP 503.
Inline and background refresh both submit a refresh_token grant to the OAuth token endpoint, not the inference upstream. Inference quota classification is not used for refresh responses.

Request-time selection waits for refresh when a selectable candidate is expired or within a hard-coded 60 seconds of expiry; it returns the new token on success or skips the candidate on failure without falling back to the old access token.

The background task skips its immediate first tick and scans a snapshot of current pool membership, including disabled and cooling members but not credential-only IDs; it skips missing credentials and those beyond the refresh threshold. The shipped check interval is 300 seconds and threshold is 900 seconds.

For refresh, HTTP 401/403 or a top-level JSON error of invalid_grant on a non-success response is permanent and disables the account in both paths; other refresh failures leave status unchanged, including transport errors, ordinary 429/5xx, and malformed success responses. Inline failures advance the scan and background failures can be retried on later cycles.
Both refresh paths update access, returned refresh token and expiry together; successful background refresh does not reactivate a disabled member or cancel a cooldown.

One CredentialStore mutex protects in-process snapshots, mutations and writes; the full JSON is written to a same-directory temporary file, chmodded to 0600 on Unix, and renamed atomically. This is neither cross-process coordination nor serialization of refresh HTTP requests, which can use the same refresh token concurrently.

Credential mutations precede persistence with no rollback. A failed refresh write can leave rotated tokens in memory and older tokens on disk; inline selection still returns the new access token, and background refresh warns about persistence but still increments its success counter.

Enrollment attempts to save the credential before adding the member and returns an error without adding it to the pool if persistence fails; adding a member sets or resets its runtime status to Available.

Admin deletion removes the runtime member first and returns removal success even if the credential removal write fails; if startup membership comes from stored IDs, a credential left on disk can restore the deleted member on restart.

Pool regression tests check rotation order, skip rules and lazy cooldown expiry; the expired-token test uses the real token endpoint and verifies fallback to a different member without requiring a permanent-failure outcome.

Classifier unit tests distinguish inference quota and token refresh errors, and local mock-upstream proxy tests assert quota failover followed by success and immediate return of inference 401 without a second call.
Store tests cover missing-file creation, save/load round-trip and concurrent JSON writes using a single shared store, not refresh HTTP serialization.
